channel.title: Nicotine Science and Policy
channel.description: Daily digest of views, debates and discussions on nicotine science, policy, regulation and advocacy.

item.title: "My Best Friend"
item.description: Sometimes harm reduction begins with one person who refuses to give up on someone else. Behind the evidence, policy arguments and product categories are people who smoke, people who love them, and people trying to keep them alive long enough to find a safer path. Tobacco harm reduction is often discussed as a technical issue, but its urgency is deeply human. The goal is not to win an argument about nicotine — it is to reduce harm for real people. (Published on August 04, 2026bysubstack.com)

item.title: TAM: Ottawa's proposed vape flavour ban ignores science and punishes 2 million adult Canadians
item.description: Two million adult Canadians should not become collateral damage in a policy designed around fear. Ottawa’s proposed vape flavour ban risks removing the products that many adults rely on to stay away from cigarettes. Science should guide regulation: protect young people through enforcement and age controls, but do not erase the flavours that help make switching work. A policy that punishes adult smokers for choosing a lower-risk option is not harm reduction. (Published on August 04, 2026bywesternstandard.news)

item.title: Time to reform Australia’s failed policy on smoking and vaping
item.description: Australia’s smoking and vaping policy has created a system where cigarettes remain easy to buy, while safer alternatives are treated as a problem to be contained. That contradiction has weakened trust, fuelled illicit supply and made switching harder for adults who smoke. Reform should start with a simple principle: regulate nicotine products according to risk, not political discomfort. A policy that keeps the most harmful product as the easiest option is not protecting public health. (Published on August 04, 2026bypearlsandirritations.com)

item.title: The Difference Between Quitting Nicotine and Ending Smoking
item.description: Quitting nicotine and quitting smoking are not the same public health outcome. A person may continue using nicotine while dramatically reducing exposure to the toxicants created by burning tobacco. That distinction matters because insisting on nicotine abstinence as the only acceptable goal can overlook meaningful reductions in disease risk. For many smokers, the first priority should be leaving combustion behind — even if nicotine use does not end immediately. (Published on August 04, 2026bysubstack.com)

item.title: India continues punishing vapers, while having high tobacco usage rates
item.description: India’s tobacco burden remains enormous, yet people who vape continue to face punishment instead of proportionate policy. Criminalising or heavily restricting lower-risk alternatives does not make nicotine demand disappear; it narrows the legal routes away from combustible tobacco. A country with high tobacco use needs more harm reduction, not fewer options for adults trying to reduce risk. Public health should focus on moving people away from the deadliest products, not penalising those who choose a safer path. (Published on August 04, 2026byworldvapersalliance.com)
